ideas.title: What If Your Calendar Skipped Eleven Dates Tonight?
ideas.premise: What if today your calendar date jumped from September 2 to September 14 under the documented calendar reform?

cast_gags.crow: Opens the tower book on the dates the calendar actually labels.
cast_gags.pip: Tries to find an imagined appointment on a skipped date label.
cast_gags.mia: Distinguishes skipped labels from eleven vanished natural days.
cast_gags.rex: Insists his fictional meeting schedule still makes sense.
cast_gags.timmy: Flips the calendar faster than Rex can point.

rationale.curiosity: A date jump creates a strong question with a specific primary-law answer.
rationale.cast_comedy: Conflicting appointments let each character cause the next complication.
rationale.modern_contrast: A smartphone calendar makes the reform visible without claiming lost wages or riots.
rationale.primary_sources: The enacted text specifies the date numbering; verify access and anchors.

ideas.title: What If Your Tax Receipt Was a Piece of Wood?
ideas.premise: What if today your official payment receipt had to be a notched wooden tally?
ideas.benchmark_query: wooden tally sticks government loans history

cast_gags.crow: Opens a file whose receipt is longer than the desk.
cast_gags.pip: Tries to fit an imagined wooden receipt into a modern wallet.
cast_gags.mia: Checks the official record rather than calling it primitive or counterfeit.
cast_gags.rex: Demands that Pip keep the original timber.
cast_gags.timmy: Brings an absurdly oversized receipt rack.

rationale.curiosity: A familiar receipt becomes a surprising physical object.
rationale.cast_comedy: Wallet, desk and archive scale support physical comedy without inventing fiscal rules.
rationale.modern_contrast: Modern digital record keeping contrasts with a documented medieval receipt.
rationale.primary_sources: A museum-held 1694 loan tally is accessible. The earlier medieval catalogue page failed; no inaccessible 1293 evidence is presented as verified.

ideas.title: What If Your Shopping Cart Still Used 240 Pennies per Pound?
ideas.premise: What if today a shopping checkout still had to calculate twelve pennies per shilling and twenty shillings per pound?

cast_gags.crow: Opens a ledger and watches the checkout change columns.
cast_gags.pip: Tries to pay for one imagined modern grocery basket.
cast_gags.mia: Does the conversion correctly and exposes the needless mental load.
cast_gags.rex: Insists that every checkout subtotal use the old units.
cast_gags.timmy: Produces a modern calculator with absurdly too few buttons.

rationale.curiosity: A routine checkout gains an unfamiliar but concrete arithmetic system.
rationale.cast_comedy: Different fixed roles can react to one escalating calculation rather than a fact list.
rationale.modern_contrast: Online shopping provides a clear modern contrast; no invented historical prices are needed.
rationale.primary_sources: The museum presents period accounts and a design brief; differentiate the article from the reproduced records.

sources.locator: Decimalisation; old accounts and Royal Mint design brief, November 1966
anchors: twelve pennies to the shilling and twenty shillings to the pound

ideas.title: What If Every Window Came With a Tax Bill?
ideas.premise: What if today the number of windows in your home determined a household tax?

cast_gags.crow: Opens an archive book shaped like a property listing, then questions the sales pitch.
cast_gags.pip: Chooses between daylight and an imagined modern tax bill.
cast_gags.mia: Points out the absurd incentive without inventing a tax rate.
cast_gags.rex: Counts windows with a smiling clipboard.
cast_gags.timmy: Adds a toy window just as Rex finishes counting.

rationale.curiosity: The everyday value of daylight conflicts with a documented tax base.
rationale.cast_comedy: Counting visible windows gives the five fixed roles distinct physical actions.
rationale.modern_contrast: An imagined apartment viewing makes a historical household duty legible.
rationale.primary_sources: An actual dated receipt and archival reference are available; verify the page before production.

ideas.title: What If Buying Socks Needed Coupons as Well as Money?
ideas.premise: What if today an online clothing checkout demanded ration coupons as well as money?

cast_gags.crow: Opens a clothing catalogue that turns into the archive notice.
cast_gags.pip: Reaches a fictional online checkout with money but no usable coupons.
cast_gags.mia: Points to the actual rule and rejects made-up coupon quantities.
cast_gags.rex: Adds another imaginary checkout requirement with a false smile.
cast_gags.timmy: Offers tiny paper coupons for an oversized pair of socks.

rationale.curiosity: The extra non-cash condition creates an immediate curiosity gap.
rationale.cast_comedy: Checkout, sock size and coupon handling offer distinct visual consequences.
rationale.modern_contrast: Modern online retail is contrasted with a documented wartime purchase condition.
rationale.primary_sources: The archive reproduces a contemporary notice; no numerical allowance is inferred.

sources.locator: Fair Shares: contemporary clothing-rationing notice/transcript, June 1941
anchors: you will have to present coupons
